weak: We'd pick long context when the knowledge is small, queried often and cacheable. A handbook of 150 short clauses ran about 7,200 input tokens a query against roughly 260 for retrieval at k of 4, around 28 times the cost on an uncached read. With a prompt cache the read drops to about a tenth, and below some size the index isn't worth building. I'd work out the crossover from knowledge base size, query rate and cache hit rate, and use retrieval for anything that changes daily.

Because showing the residual keeps the reconciliation honest and lets the team trust the total. A residual of 1.9 percent is within normal tolerance for metered billing, so it can be labelled and left on the page while the team reconciles the rest. A labelled line that is allowed to shrink over time is a sign the model is working.

I start from the break-even point rather than a rule of thumb. Cost per thousand requests is the hourly price divided by requests served per hour at the utilisation I expect. On an assumed $2.50 an hour and 50 requests a second, that is $0.014 per thousand at full load and about $0.69 at 2 percent, which is above the API's price. The sources I read put the floor near 30 percent. I would measure average and peak demand over a month, check the utilisation against that threshold, and then decide. Smoothing the load can bring the number up, so I would treat it as part of the plan.

Price it from the cost distribution, not the average. Run costs for agents are heavy-tailed, so a flat per-run price leaves the expensive runs underwater and overcharges the cheap ones. I would set the unit to something the customer controls, like a completed task with a per-run ceiling, and test the price against the 90th-percentile cost before anything else. The margin floor should hold at p90, since that is where the real exposure sits.

We'd know a limit is working from three numbers: how often runs hit it, how much spend sits in those runs, and how far they overshoot the limit. If a limit fires on around 40 percent of runs, the price is badly sized and people will route around it. If it never fires, it's either set too high or protecting nothing. I'd also log why each run stopped, so a cap hit, a breaker trip and a manual kill are kept separate, because they point to different fixes.

The per-run ceiling in the agent loop, since that is where actual usage is visible and a run can be stopped while spend is still happening. The user, team and global limits in the gateway, because the tags live there and the check does not rely on the agent code being correct. The provider's hard limit as a final backstop. A system prompt saying "keep costs low" is useful guidance, but it is not a control.

One ledger with a state for each saving, identified, committed or realised, and a baseline for each. In my lab caching saved 87 percent and retrieval 95.8 percent against the same baseline, and the two stacked cleanly. I would credit each lever with its full measured saving and reconcile the total to the invoice each month.

By giving the vignettes to people who have not read the checklist and seeing whether they pick the right ones. I'd run a small panel of readers blind to the labels, and the agreement rate tells me whether the checklist is usable. Where readers disagree, the misses show me which categories overlap. I would then tighten the categories or reword the controls, whichever the disagreements point at.

I would not conclude that a dollar cap is free. In my lab it looked cheap because the capped runs mostly stopped early, on one small model and one synthetic task, with 60 runs per policy. The accuracy drop at the main cap, about 5 points, was within the noise, so I can only say no meaningful loss was detected there. The cap at half that value did cost accuracy, so the claim only holds at or above $0.012. I did not test a gateway or pre-flight cost estimates, and I would not claim either one reduces spend without testing it on a real workload.

I would compare the multi-agent design against the strongest single-agent version on the same tasks and track cost per accepted outcome and wall time. If the pipeline costs more and gives little gain in either outcome or time, the justification has to come from a task property a single agent cannot handle, like work that exceeds one context window. In one study of six architectures, a planner, coder and reviewer pipeline cost 3.22 times a single strong call while solving more tasks in total, so the extra spend was easy to defend.

When the label set is stable, volume is high and labelled data exists. One study found fine-tuned encoders cut inference cost by one to two orders of magnitude at January 2026 prices, so the saving is large enough to justify the build. The boundary is a taxonomy that changes often, where retraining erases the saving.

I handle an assumption by labelling it on the page with its basis and owner, then replacing it with a measurement once that is cheap to do. In the pack, the human cost per handoff was an assumption. The sensitivity table showed it moved the loaded cost by roughly four times across a $3 to $12 range, so it is the first thing I would measure, using a timed sample of human-handled tickets. The rework rate moved the total by only about six percent, so measuring it can wait. Executives tend to remember the headline number and forget the footnote, so I put the basis in its own column next to every figure, and the total reconciles to the invoice.

For an acquisition like this, I'd treat the acquired company's tags and hierarchy as an input to map, not something to overwrite. The acquired products become cost objects with their own start dates in the hierarchy table, owned by a new group. I'd maintain a translation table from the acquired tags and team names to our identifiers, recording the date each mapping was made. Pre-acquisition history stays as it was, since those costs weren't ours to restate. For the first quarter I'd report the acquired spend as a separate line so that any jump shows up as an acquisition rather than organic growth. Their credentials move behind our gateway on a schedule, and anything unregistered sits in the review queue until it's moved. Once the mapping covers all the active products and keys, the transition can close. For a small acquisition with one product and a few keys, a single mapping and a one-month transition are enough.

The check reserves the estimate against each applicable scope in sequence, starting with the narrowest one, and only moves on to the next scope if the current reservation succeeds. After the call it commits the actual cost and releases the unused reserve, and on a failed call it releases everything it holds. Reporting the scope that blocked the call tells the user which limit to discuss. My class tests that a refusal at one scope leaves no reservation at another, and a production version would need a shared store to hold the counters.

A retry is a repeat of a failed call, made on purpose and capped, usually with backoff, so the system recovers from a transient error. A loop is an agent repeating an action, or bouncing between two actions, without moving the task forward, and it runs without limit unless the harness sets one. I spot loops in the trace by looking for a repeated action signature, an alternating pair of calls, or a run of steps that add no new information. Treating the signal as a candidate for review and a first-step response, like a nudge to the model, avoids killing runs that were just slow.

I define forecast error as the absolute difference between the forecast and the actual for a stated period, divided by the actual. I always quote the horizon as well, meaning how many days before the period the forecast was made, since an error without a horizon is not comparable to anything else. Growth matters here: with spend rising 20 percent a month, a forecast that simply carries last month's level forward will come in low, and I can check how much of an observed error that growth explains with some quick arithmetic. I keep the unit explicit too, because a monthly total can look accurate while large errors offset each other across products or regions. In practice I report error per service and per account so the numbers stay honest. For flat, contract-driven spend the carry-forward forecast is often nearly right, so the metric stops telling us much, and that is the point where I would switch to a different check.

Attribution coverage is the share of spend that carries an owner. Most teams report the percentage of cost lines that have a cost-center or team tag, and that number is useful for seeing where tagging discipline stands. It falls short in one place. It is measured against the count of lines, so a few large untagged lines barely move it. On the October fixture, roughly half the lines are tagged, which looks healthy and hides that the untagged lines hold most of the dollars. I report coverage by dollar value and show the lines that drive the gap, so the reader sees which owners to chase first. The number is strongest for a company with a single product and a single account, where tags are complete by construction and the real difficulty becomes allocating shared infrastructure such as networking and support.
